Senses.Explanation: To descend from the teaching seat. In the Chan record this is the standard visible close of a formal teaching-seat appearance: the person who mounted the seat may finish speaking, shout, strike or plant an implement, remain silent, or answer a demand by leaving. The action is not interchangeable with the preceding speech. Shakyamuni Buddha descends after Manjusri's sounding-block declaration in one Five Lamps scene and after his own refusal to preach in another. Tianyi Yihuai shouts and descends; Feiyin Tongrong descends only after the chief seat gives the closing declaration; and Langting Jingting says of passing geese, “They have passed,” before descending. Yaoshan Weiyan mounts the seat, remains silent, descends, and only afterward answers the rector in his quarters. When Zhaozhou Congshen asks Nanquan Puyuan to speak apart from the four propositions and hundred negations, Nanquan descends and returns to his quarters. The Linji Yixuan–Mayu Baoche exchange makes the actors especially important: Mayu first pulls Linji down and takes the seat, Linji then pulls Mayu down and retakes it, and Linji finally descends after Mayu leaves. Juelang Daosheng is preparing to descend when a lay questioner introduced as Huang Gong tells him, “Please step down.” These formal endings, commands, and forcible removals all preserve the same concrete movement away from the seat.

Senses.Note: Only one clear allowlisted occurrence of the contiguous upper-seat/lower-seat pair was found. The longer expression “lower-seat phrase” remains a nested lexical object and is not counted as another witness for this noun. Senses.Explanation: A rare nominal use for the lower of two seating positions, rather than the act of descending. In a Complete Collection of the Five Lamps encounter, Censor Wang first asks whether the bow is southern or northern and then whether it is from the upper or lower seat. Huayan Yu answers that neither end adheres and the middle is not secure either. The paired upper/lower alternatives make a seating-position referent explicit; the passage does not describe anyone leaving a seat.

Senses.Explanation: To step down from the teaching seat is a visible move in a public encounter. Xiuxi descends and is seized after two steps; Zhaozhou descends to inspect a questioner; Yungai Zhi descends and spreads his hands to Jiufeng; Baizhang Weizheng separately descends and spreads his hands after the community requests the promised teaching. The movement is part of each answer, not the ending of an ordinary sitting session.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Source record (J/J39/J39nB454.xml). Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Pinjixiang (頻吉祥禪師語錄): Pinjixiang Zhixiang says earlier figures established ten headings from searching for the ox through seeing tracks because students lacked a secure footing.

Senses.Explanation: Search for the ox is the opening action in Chan oxherding sequences and a reusable encounter image: the seeker enters the wilds looking for an animal said never truly to have been lost, follows traces, and may still be challenged for turning the search into a staged route. Konggu Daocheng receives the question 'searching for the ox without seeing tracks—what then?' and answers with an unbound calf amid wild grass before correcting the questioner's claimed sight. Yezhu Fuhui writes two search verses: staff in hand amid spring mountains and a long search that again ends with an empty mountain and crying birds. Buhui Fatong, Miyin Zhenchuan, and other oxherding authors label the first stage entering the mountains or parting grass to seek the ox. Zhe'an Jingfan raises the older line that searching for the ox requires visiting its tracks, then criticizes inherited talk of mind and nature. The image is thus both an ordered picture-stage and material that masters can question or reject; those are deployments of one search, not separate senses.

Senses.Note: Any criticism is reported from its complete line rather than built into the literal compound.

Senses.Explanation: See through means to discern past a displayed answer, case, verbal performance, or apparent obstruction so that it no longer deceives or confines the observer. Zen records also make the phrase answerable in public: a monastic’s claim to have “seen through” is challenged by Tianyin, and Yinyuan asks where the seeing-through occurred. Masters use it both as their own capping verdict and as a claim about another person, so the phrase marks asserted exposure, not proof that the assertion succeeded.

SearchAliases: look at the word or saying
Senses.Explanation: To look at a saying is to direct attention to the word, question, or conversational thread singled out in a record. The compound often occurs in the longer phrase ‘look at the saying’s head’, where the local wording determines whether English says word, saying, question, or thread. One recorded questioner seeks written direction because the saying he was looking at had not opened to him. The records also criticize the activity: Mingben reports people calling it ‘doing work’ and rejects their appeal to direct transmission; Yuancheng says an old hunter neither did work nor looked at a saying before answering that there was ‘no place to set a hand,’ contrasting this with looking around at one’s selected saying. The Chan bend is an ordinary act of looking directed at actual words in exchanges and itself subjected to public criticism.
